claims.text: Increasing oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature operation enhances short-range chemical ordering at nanoparticle surfaces.
Enhanced surface short-range chemical ordering raises local atomic diffusion barriers.
The raised diffusion barriers suppress phase segregation.
Oxygen-induced ordering stabilizes multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under catalytic conditions.
The initial nanoparticles have a nominally random elemental distribution with slight short-range ordering.
Oxygen adsorbate interactions mediate short-range chemical ordering at nanoparticle surfaces.
Adsorbed oxygen encourages short-range atomic rearrangements at nanoparticle surfaces.
Oxygen-induced rearrangements reduce atomic mobility by increasing diffusion barriers.
Reduced atomic mobility inhibits both phase segregation and coarsening during high-temperature exposure.
Nanoparticles exposed to higher oxygen partial pressure will develop more pronounced short-range ordering than nanoparticles heated under inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticles exposed to higher oxygen partial pressure will show less compositional drift than inert-atmosphere controls.
Nanoparticles exposed to higher oxygen partial pressure will undergo less phase segregation over time than inert-atmosphere controls.
Oxygen chemical potential or partial pressure can strongly affect the phase stability of multicomponent materials.
Short-range chemical ordering in compositionally complex alloys varies with temperature and can accompany phase transformation.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies within 773–1173 K to near-equiatomic, low-noble-metal nanoparticles.
At temperatures outside 773–1173 K, the proposed behavior may deviate.
Overly oxidative conditions may cause over-oxidation and deviation from the proposed stabilization behavior.
The oxygen partial-pressure threshold for optimal stabilization is not yet quantitatively known.
The magnitude of the proposed stabilization effect is not yet quantitatively known.
Failure of increasing oxygen partial pressure to enhance ordering or reduce segregation relative to an inert control would falsify the hypothesis.
